A1.justification: Both PDFs contain the same research work with readable text, figures, tables, equations, and Appendices A–I. Pages 2–21 have identical extracted text and rendered appearance. First-page differences are confined to affiliation and version/date metadata.

before.justification: v1 reports original security and functionality evaluations on CyberSecEval 2 and HumanEval, efficiency comparisons, ablations, and appendix case analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains the original experimental results, including benchmark comparisons in Tables 2–3 and supplementary analyses in the appendices.

M1.justification: The revision-trigger tokens, substring-constrained localization, patch generation, deterministic renderer, semantic initialization, and training objectives are identical.

E1.justification: Both versions retain the same CVE-derived alignment data, C/C++ training coverage, six-language CyberSecEval 2 evaluation, and C/C++ HumanEval evaluation.

E2.justification: Comparator membership is unchanged: Tables 2–3 retain the base models, SafeCoder, ProSec, two post-hoc agent variants, and patch-only SFT comparison.

E3.justification: Evaluation metrics, model configurations, sample sizes, training settings, and agent testing procedures are unchanged in Sections 5–7 and Appendices C–G.

E4.justification: The same data-quality, revision-removal, constrained-localization, alignment, and trigger-calibration analyses remain. Appendices A, D, H, and I retain their localization, initialization, per-CWE, case-study, and failure analyses.

E5.justification: Statistical reporting is identical, including the p<0.01 statement in Section 6 and the statistically indistinguishable comparison in Section 7.1. No run-count, seed, uncertainty-reporting, or statistical-testing information changes.

E6.justification: All numerical and qualitative findings match across the main text and appendices. For example, Table 2 retains Qwen2.5-7B Stream of Revision security pass rates of 73.76% for C and 83.47% for C++.

T1.justification: The task definitions, revision formalization, constrained-decoding equations, localized-vulnerability assumptions, and efficiency derivations remain identical, including Appendices A–C.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same claims about revision within autoregressive decoding, data efficiency, security improvement, utility preservation, and low inference overhead.

C2.justification: Interpretations of cross-language transfer, data quality, and calibration are unchanged. The multi-hunk localization limitation in Appendix A and incomplete-patch, parser, and residual-security limitations in Appendix I are also retained.

D1.justification: Token initialization, hyperparameters, A100 hardware, data-construction instructions, and agent prompts in Appendices D–G are identical. No code or data access disclosure changes.

R1.justification: Section 8 and the reference list are identical. Positioning relative to security alignment, agentic repair, constrained generation, and editing or diffusion models is unchanged.

P1.justification: Page 1 changes the Huazhong affiliation from School of Computer Science and Technology to School of Cyber Science and Engineering, and updates the preprint date and arXiv version/date stamp. Scientific wording and document structure are unchanged.

P2.justification: Figures 1–5 and Tables 1–5 retain identical designs, captions, contents, and placement. The first-page metadata edits preserve the document layout.

improvement.justification: v2 updates only affiliation and version/date metadata. The scientific content, supporting evidence, explanations, limitations, reproducibility details, and visual presentation remain unchanged throughout the main text and appendices, establishing no meaningful overall quality difference.
